| [NOTE-558](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-558.md) | Phase Shifts, Herbivory, and the Resilience of Coral Reefs to Climate Change | Four roofless 25 m² cages on Orpheus Island's reef crest kept large and medium fishes out for 30 months after the 1998 bleaching, against four partial cages and four open plots. | [NOTE-571](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-571.md) | Catastrophic regime shifts in ecosystems: linking theory to observation | A review of how to tell whether an ecosystem has alternative stable states. Field patterns (jumps, multimodality, dual relationships) are suggestive and never conclusive, since a stepwise driver or a simple threshold produces them too. Experiments can come close to proof: initial-state dependence, lasting shifts after temporary disturbance, and hysteresis. Models show positive feedback must be strong enough. | Read |
| [NOTE-572](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-572.md) | Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems | Ecological theory had equated stability with behaviour near equilibrium. Holling separates stability (return to equilibrium) from resilience (the capacity to absorb change and persist, set by the domain of attraction), shows they can trade off in lakes, forests, insects and fish, and warns that managing for constant yield can erode resilience. | Read |

| [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md) | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale — The evolution of dependence and cohesion in incipient endosymbioses | An adaptive-dynamics model in which hosts, symbionts and host–symbiont collectives are three populations. Each partner has an "obligacy" (investment in collective rather than free-living growth) and an "adhesion" (investment in synchronized, collective reproduction). The faster-growing partner, the symbiont, becomes fully obligate first. What the host's obligacy then does depends on within-collective births and deaths: it stays, rises to full dependence, or falls to none. Obligacy rises only if the collective's carrying capacity is high enough; collective growth rate does not matter. Early on, dependence evolves ahead of cohesion. That last result holds for the trait mapping the authors chose, and their own Table S1 reverses it under the opposite mapping. The authors say the available data can neither confirm nor refute it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md) | Morris, Lenski & Zinser — The Black Queen Hypothesis | Proposes that in free-living microbes, losing a costly function whose product leaks to neighbours is favoured by ordinary individual selection, and the loss runs until the remaining producers ("helpers") just supply the community, leaving most cells ("beneficiaries") dependent on a rare few. No relatedness, cooperation or collective is needed, only leakiness and frequency dependence. The one worked case is the loss of catalase-peroxidase (katG) in Prochlorococcus, which cannot survive the hydrogen peroxide that its community removes. The other cases are suggestions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1213](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1213.md) | McCutcheon, Garber, Spencer & Warren — How do bacterial endosymbionts work with so few genes? | An essay on the endosymbionts with genomes under about 200 kb, which the authors call "tipping-point endosymbionts". Below about 400 kb, symbionts almost always lose the genes to build their own envelope and to move proteins across it. Below about 200 kb, even translation erodes: ribosomal proteins, tRNAs and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases go. Their proteomes are among the most compositionally biased in bacteria. The paper asks four questions it cannot answer: where their membranes, transporters, missing translation parts and protein stability come from. Its best guess is from the host, as in organelles. The thresholds come from a hand-picked set of genomes, and the composition analysis is called preliminary. | Read |
| [NOTE-1235](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1235.md) | Campbell et al. — Changes in endosymbiont complexity drive host-level compensatory adaptations in cicadas | In cicadas whose endosymbiont Hodgkinia has split into many lineages, each essential, the mother must put every lineage into every egg. A simulation shows that random transmission would need far more cells as lineages multiply and grow uneven. Counts in eggs of four species find Sulcia numbers roughly constant, and Hodgkinia numbers up to about six times higher in Magicicada septendecim than in a single-lineage species. Amplicon sequencing found every tracked Hodgkinia genotype in every egg sampled. The transmission route looks the same under the light microscope. Only M. septendecim differs significantly; the six-lineage species does not. So the compensation rests on one species. The authors call the raised titre a cost of fragmentation, and speculate that it could feed further splitting. | Read |
| [NOTE-1236](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1236.md) | Shigenobu, Watanabe, Hattori, Sakaki & Ishikawa — Genome sequence of the endocellular bacterial symbiont of aphids Buchnera sp. APS | The first complete genome of an obligate insect endosymbiont. Buchnera APS, from the pea aphid, has a 640,681-bp chromosome with 583 ORFs and two small plasmids. It is a subset of the E. coli gene set, produced by loss from a larger common ancestor. It keeps the pathways for the amino acids its host cannot make, lacks almost all of those the host can, and draws some precursors from the host, so the two partners' pathways interlock. It also lacks phospholipid and lipopolysaccharide synthesis, almost all transcriptional regulators, and recA and uvrABC. The authors infer that it can live only in the bacteriocyte and compare it to an organelle. Everything here is read from gene content; no experiment on the symbiont is reported, and the host's dependence is asserted from the literature, not shown. | Read |
| [NOTE-1241](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1241.md) | Sørensen, Stiller, Kröninger & Nowack — Protein import into bacterial endosymbionts and evolving organelles | A review of the evidence that hosts import their own proteins into bacterial endosymbionts, which has long been taken to mark an organelle off from an endosymbiont. Import of hundreds of nucleus-encoded proteins is established, by proteomics of isolated endosymbionts, in two systems only: the chromatophore of Paulinella and the nitroplast of Braarudosphaera. In both, the imported proteins come mostly from the host's own genes and from bacteria other than the endosymbiont, and the authors say that gene transfer from the endosymbiont "is not a precondition" for genetic integration. Elsewhere, in a trypanosomatid, a diatom and four insects, there are one to seven imported or targeted proteins per system, each found by antibodies or proteomics. The authors propose an order, effector proteins first and dependence on an imported redundant protein second, which they call plausible on limited data. The import mechanisms are almost entirely unknown. | Read |
